entry.sum: An algorithm is a finite, unambiguous procedure that turns every valid input into the correct output after finitely many steps. Its time complexity counts how many basic operations it performs, as a function of the input size $n$, in the worst case; asymptotic notation then compares algorithms by growth rate, for example $O(\log n)$ for binary search against $\Theta(n\log n)$ for merge sort and $\Theta(n^2)$ for insertion sort.
key: \text{binary search in a sorted list of } n \text{ items uses at most } \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + 1 \text{ comparisons}
T(n) = 2T(n/2) + \Theta(n) \implies T(n) = \Theta(n \log n)
\text{every comparison sort needs at least } \lceil \log_2 n! \rceil = \Theta(n\log n) \text{ comparisons in the worst case}
entry.why: For a million items, an $n\log_2 n$ algorithm does about $2\times 10^7$ basic steps while an $n^2$ one does $10^{12}$: the difference between a fraction of a second and many minutes. Complexity analysis is how one predicts this before running anything, and it underlies questions such as whether factoring is hard enough to keep RSA safe.

links.note: Running times of recursive algorithms are recurrence relations, solved with the same telescoping, induction and generating-function methods used for counting problems.
The Euclidean algorithm and fast modular exponentiation run in a number of steps proportional to the number of digits, which is what makes computational number theory practical.
Dynamic programming solves discrete optimisation problems such as shortest routes and knapsack packing by combining optimal answers to smaller subproblems.

refs: Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest & Stein, Introduction to Algorithms
Rosen, Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications
Kleinberg & Tardos, Algorithm Design

blocks.body:
Suppose a phone book holds a million names in alphabetical order and you want one particular name. Reading from the top could take a million looks. Opening at the middle, deciding which half the name is in, and repeating takes at most 20 looks. Both methods are correct; one is fifty thousand times faster in the worst case.

An algorithm is a recipe a machine could follow without judgement; its complexity counts the work it does as a function of the input size. With careful counting, recurrences and [[asymptotics|asymptotic notation]] one can predict running times, prove algorithms correct, and sometimes prove that no algorithm can do better.

blocks.title: What counts as an algorithm
blocks.body:
An algorithm takes an input from some specified set, performs a finite sequence of precisely defined steps, and stops with an output. Five properties are usually asked for: the input and output are specified; each step is unambiguous; each step can actually be carried out; the procedure always stops; and the output is correct for every valid input.

A first example: find the largest entry of a list $a_1, \dots, a_n$. Set $m = a_1$. For $i = 2, \dots, n$, if $a_i > m$, replace $m$ by $a_i$. Output $m$.

Why is this correct? Use a loop invariant: after the step for index $i$, the value $m$ is the largest of $a_1, \dots, a_i$. It holds after the start (with $i = 1$), and if it holds after step $i-1$ then step $i$ keeps it true, because the new $m$ is $\max(m, a_i)$. By [[induction]] it holds after step $n$, which is exactly the claim. Most correctness proofs for loops have this shape.

How much work does it do? Exactly $n - 1$ comparisons, whatever the input. Counting one kind of basic operation (comparisons, multiplications, array reads) and ignoring the rest is the standard simplification: it changes the true running time only by a constant factor, and constant factors depend on the machine anyway.

blocks.title: Worst-case time complexity
blocks.body:
Fix a notion of input size $n$ (the length of a list, the number of digits of a number, the number of vertices of a graph) and a basic operation. The worst-case time complexity of an algorithm is the function

$$T(n) = \max\{\text{number of basic operations on input } x : x \text{ has size } n\}.$$

The average-case complexity replaces the maximum by an average over a stated probability distribution on inputs of size $n$. In both cases we usually only record the growth rate, writing $T(n) = O(g(n))$ or $T(n) = \Theta(g(n))$.

In words: $T(n)$ is a guarantee. No input of size $n$ makes the algorithm do more than $T(n)$ basic steps.

blocks.title: Counting operations and growth rates
blocks.body:
Linear search looks for a target $t$ in a list by checking $a_1, a_2, \dots$ in turn. In the worst case (the target is last, or absent) it makes $n$ comparisons, so $T(n) = n$. If the target is present and equally likely to be in each position, the average is $(n+1)/2$: still linear.

Insertion sort builds a sorted list one item at a time, sliding each new item left past the larger items before it. If the input is in decreasing order, item number $k$ is compared with all $k - 1$ items before it, so the total is $1 + 2 + \cdots + (n-1) = n(n-1)/2$ comparisons. That is $\Theta(n^2)$.

Rounded values show why growth rate is what matters:

- $n = 10$: $\log_2 n \approx 3.3$, $n \log_2 n \approx 33$, $n^2 = 100$, $2^n = 1024$.
- $n = 1000$: $\log_2 n \approx 10$, $n \log_2 n \approx 9966$, $n^2 = 10^6$, $2^n \approx 1.07 \times 10^{301}$.
- $n = 10^6$: $\log_2 n \approx 19.9$, $n \log_2 n \approx 2.0 \times 10^7$, $n^2 = 10^{12}$.

An algorithm is called polynomial-time if $T(n) = O(n^k)$ for some fixed $k$, where $n$ is the length of the input written out in symbols. Exponential algorithms such as trying all $2^n$ subsets become hopeless around $n = 60$ or so.

blocks.title: Binary search
blocks.body:
Let $a_1 < a_2 < \cdots < a_n$ be sorted and let $t$ be a target. Binary search compares $t$ with the middle entry $a_m$, $m = \lfloor (1+n)/2 \rfloor$; it stops if $t = a_m$, and otherwise repeats on $a_1, \dots, a_{m-1}$ (if $t < a_m$) or on $a_{m+1}, \dots, a_n$ (if $t > a_m$), stopping with "absent" when the range is empty. In the worst case it makes exactly

$$C(n) = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + 1$$

three-way comparisons (each comparison decides $<$, $=$ or $>$), which is the number of binary digits of $n$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
After one comparison the two possible sub-ranges have $m - 1 = \lfloor (n-1)/2 \rfloor$ and $n - m = \lceil (n-1)/2 \rceil = \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ entries. The second is at least as large. An adversary can always answer so that the search continues in the larger range, and $C$ is nondecreasing (which follows from the recurrence below by strong induction), so with $C(0) = 0$,

$$C(n) = 1 + C(\lfloor n/2 \rfloor) \quad (n \ge 1).$$

Now let $b(n)$ be the number of binary digits of $n \ge 1$, with $b(0) = 0$. Deleting the last binary digit of $n$ gives $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$, so $b(n) = 1 + b(\lfloor n/2 \rfloor)$. The functions $C$ and $b$ satisfy the same recurrence with the same starting value, so by strong induction $C(n) = b(n)$ for all $n$. Finally, if $2^k \le n < 2^{k+1}$ then $n$ has $k + 1$ binary digits and $k = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$. For a million items this gives $C(10^6) = 20$.

blocks.title: Divide and conquer, and recurrences
blocks.body:
Merge sort splits a list of $n$ items into halves of sizes $\lceil n/2 \rceil$ and $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$, sorts each half recursively, then merges. Merging two sorted lists of lengths $p$ and $q$ is easy: repeatedly compare the two front items and move the smaller one to the output. Each comparison outputs one item, and when one list runs out the rest of the other is copied without comparisons, so at most $p + q - 1$ comparisons are needed. The worst-case number of comparisons therefore obeys

$$M(1) = 0, \qquad M(n) = M(\lceil n/2 \rceil) + M(\lfloor n/2 \rfloor) + n - 1.$$

For small $n$: $M(2) = 1$, $M(3) = 3$, $M(4) = 5$, $M(5) = 8$, $M(8) = 17$.

Many divide-and-conquer recurrences have the form $T(n) = a\,T(n/b) + f(n)$: split into $a$ subproblems of size $n/b$ and spend $f(n)$ on splitting and combining. Picture the recursion as a tree. Level $j$ has $a^j$ subproblems of size $n/b^j$, so if $f(n) = c\,n^d$ the work on level $j$ is $c\,n^d (a/b^d)^j$. This is a geometric series in $j$ with ratio $r = a/b^d$. If $r < 1$ the top level dominates, if $r = 1$ all $\log_b n$ levels contribute equally, and if $r > 1$ the bottom level (the $n^{\log_b a}$ leaves) dominates. This picture is the content of the next theorem.

blocks.title: Master theorem (polynomial case)
blocks.body:
Let $a \ge 1$, $b > 1$, $d \ge 0$ be constants and suppose $T(n) = a\,T(n/b) + \Theta(n^d)$, with $n/b$ read as $\lfloor n/b \rfloor$ or $\lceil n/b \rceil$. Then

$$T(n) = \begin{cases} \Theta(n^d) & \text{if } d > \log_b a,\\ \Theta(n^d \log n) & \text{if } d = \log_b a,\\ \Theta(n^{\log_b a}) & \text{if } d < \log_b a. \end{cases}$$

We do not prove the general statement here (the recursion-tree argument above is its proof sketch, and the rounding needs extra care; see Cormen et al.). The next result proves the merge sort case exactly when $n$ is a power of 2.

blocks.title: Comparisons in merge sort
blocks.body: For $n = 2^k$ with $k \ge 0$, the worst-case number of comparisons of merge sort is $M(n) = n \log_2 n - n + 1$. In particular $M(n) = \Theta(n \log n)$.

blocks.title: Lower bound for comparison sorting
blocks.body: Any algorithm that sorts $n$ distinct items using only comparisons between items makes at least $\lceil \log_2 n! \rceil$ comparisons on some input. Since $\log_2 n! \ge \frac{n}{2}\log_2 \frac{n}{2}$ for $n \ge 2$, this is $\Omega(n \log n)$, so merge sort is optimal up to a constant factor.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Run the algorithm on all $n!$ orderings of the items. Its behaviour is a binary decision tree: each internal node is a comparison "is $x < y$?", the two branches are the two answers, and each leaf is a final output. Two different orderings must reach different leaves, since the correct output (the permutation that sorts them) is different. So the tree has at least $n!$ leaves. A binary tree of height $h$ has at most $2^h$ leaves (induction on $h$), so $2^h \ge n!$ and the worst case $h$ satisfies $h \ge \log_2 n!$; as $h$ is an integer, $h \ge \lceil \log_2 n! \rceil$.

For the estimate: the largest $\lceil n/2 \rceil$ factors of $n!$ are each at least $n/2$, so $n! \ge (n/2)^{n/2}$ and $\log_2 n! \ge \frac{n}{2}\log_2\frac{n}{2}$.

For $n = 5$ the bound is $\lceil \log_2 120 \rceil = 7$. Merge sort uses $M(5) = 8$ in the worst case, so it is not exactly optimal for small $n$: cleverer schemes sort 5 items in 7 comparisons.

blocks.title: Dynamic programming
blocks.body:
Some recursions are slow because they solve the same subproblem many times. The Fibonacci numbers $F_0 = 0$, $F_1 = 1$, $F_n = F_{n-1} + F_{n-2}$ illustrate this. Computing $F_n$ by literally calling the definition makes $c(n)$ calls, where $c(0) = c(1) = 1$ and $c(n) = 1 + c(n-1) + c(n-2)$. One checks by induction that $c(n) = 2F_{n+1} - 1$, which grows like $1.618^n$: computing $F_{40}$ this way takes over 300 million calls. Yet there are only $n + 1$ different subproblems $F_0, \dots, F_n$. Computing them in increasing order and storing each answer takes $n - 1$ additions.

That is dynamic programming: identify a family of subproblems (stages and states), write the answer to each in terms of smaller ones (a recurrence, often called the Bellman equation in optimisation), and fill in a table from the smallest upward. The running time is roughly (number of states) times (work per state).

A typical decision problem: with coins of values 1, 3 and 4, what is the fewest coins summing to $n$? Let $g(n)$ be that number. The last coin used is 1, 3 or 4, so

$$g(0) = 0, \qquad g(n) = 1 + \min\{g(n-c) : c \in \{1,3,4\},\ c \le n\}.$$

The table for $n = 0, 1, \dots, 10$ is $0, 1, 2, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3$. Note $g(6) = 2$ (as $3 + 3$), while the greedy rule "always take the largest coin that fits" gives $4 + 1 + 1$, three coins.

blocks.title: Fast powers
blocks.body: Computing $x^n$ by multiplying $x$ by itself takes $n - 1$ multiplications. Show that $x^{13}$ can be computed with 5 multiplications, and that in general $x^n$ needs at most $2\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$ multiplications.
blocks.solution:
Write $13 = 1101_2 = 8 + 4 + 1$. Square repeatedly: $x^2 = x\cdot x$, $x^4 = x^2 \cdot x^2$, $x^8 = x^4\cdot x^4$ (3 multiplications). Then $x^{13} = x^8 \cdot x^4 \cdot x$ (2 more). Total 5, instead of 12. For $x = 3$ this gives $3^{13} = 1594323$.

In general let $k = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$, so $n$ has $k+1$ binary digits. Computing $x^{2}, x^{4}, \dots, x^{2^k}$ takes $k$ squarings. Then $x^n$ is the product of the powers $x^{2^j}$ for which digit $j$ of $n$ is 1; there are at most $k + 1$ of them, so at most $k$ further multiplications. The total is at most $2k$.

The same method computes $a^n \bmod N$ with numbers that never exceed $N^2$, in $O(\log n)$ multiplications. This is why [[rsa]] encryption with exponents hundreds of digits long is fast.

blocks.title: Solving recurrences
blocks.body: Find the growth rate of each: (a) $T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n$, (b) $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n^2$; and (c) $T(n) = 3T(n/2) + n$, the recurrence of Karatsuba's multiplication method for $n$-digit numbers.
blocks.solution:
(a) $a = 4$, $b = 2$, $\log_2 4 = 2 > d = 1$, so the leaves dominate: $\Theta(n^2)$.

(b) $\log_2 2 = 1 < d = 2$, so the top level dominates: $\Theta(n^2)$. The two recurrences have the same answer for opposite reasons.

(c) $\log_2 3 \approx 1.585 > 1$, so $T(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_2 3})$. Schoolbook multiplication of two $n$-digit numbers takes $\Theta(n^2)$ digit operations; Karatsuba's trick of replacing four half-size products by three gives a strictly smaller exponent.

blocks.title: The best block of consecutive days
blocks.body: A list of daily gains and losses $a_1, \dots, a_n$ is given (some negative). Find the largest possible sum of a block $a_i + a_{i+1} + \cdots + a_j$ of consecutive entries (at least one entry), in $O(n)$ time. Try it on $3, -4, 5, -1, 2, -6, 4$.
blocks.solution:
Checking all $\binom{n}{2} + n$ blocks is $\Theta(n^2)$ at best. Instead, let $E_j$ be the largest sum of a block that ends exactly at position $j$. Such a block is either $a_j$ alone or a best block ending at $j-1$ extended by $a_j$, so

$$E_1 = a_1, \qquad E_j = a_j + \max(E_{j-1}, 0).$$

The answer is $\max_j E_j$, since every block ends somewhere. One pass through the list computes all $E_j$ and their running maximum: $n - 1$ steps of constant work, so $\Theta(n)$.

Correctness is the invariant "after step $j$, the stored value equals $E_j$ and the running maximum equals the best block inside $a_1, \dots, a_j$", proved by induction on $j$ exactly as for the maximum-finding algorithm.

On the given list: $E = 3, -1, 5, 4, 6, 0, 4$, so the answer is 6, from the block $5 - 1 + 2$.

blocks.body:
- $O(g)$ is only an upper bound. Saying insertion sort is $O(n^3)$ is true but useless; use $\Theta$ when you mean the exact growth rate.
- Asymptotics hide constants. For lists of 10 items, insertion sort often beats merge sort in practice. Big-O predicts what happens as $n$ grows, not at every $n$.
- Input size means the length of the input. Trial division tests whether $N$ is prime with about $\sqrt{N}$ divisions. That looks polynomial, but $N$ has about $d = \log_{10} N$ digits, and $\sqrt{N} \approx 10^{d/2}$ is exponential in $d$. See [[primality]].
- A plausible greedy rule is not a proof. The coin example above shows the largest-coin rule failing.

The [[divisibility|Euclidean algorithm]] is one of the oldest algorithms and runs in $O(\log \min(a,b))$ division steps, which follows from the Fibonacci numbers being the worst case. Breadth-first search, Dijkstra's shortest paths and minimum spanning trees on [[graph-algorithms]] are analysed with the counting methods of this page; [[network-flows]] and [[linear-programming]] go further. Recurrences for running times are solved with the tools of [[sequences]] and [[generating-functions]]. Whether every problem whose solutions can be checked quickly can also be solved quickly is the [[p-vs-np]] question, and the security of [[rsa]] and [[discrete-log]] cryptography rests on believing some problems have no fast algorithm. At the extreme, [[computability]] shows that some problems have no algorithm at all.

1. Prove by induction that the number of calls $c(n)$ made by the naive Fibonacci recursion equals $2F_{n+1} - 1$.
2. Find the worst-case number of comparisons of merge sort for $n = 6$ and $n = 7$, and compare with $\lceil \log_2 n! \rceil$.
3. Use the master theorem to find the growth of $T(n) = 7T(n/2) + n^2$ (Strassen's matrix multiplication) and of $T(n) = 2T(n/4) + \sqrt{n}$.
4. With coins 1, 5 and 12, find the smallest amount for which the greedy rule does not give the fewest coins.

from functools import lru_cache
import math
def worst(n):
    # simulate binary search on 1..n, max comparisons over all targets (present and absent)
    best=0
    for t2 in range(1,2*n+2):  # targets 0.5,1,1.5,...: even t2 means present value t2/2
        lo,hi,c=1,n,0
        while lo<=hi:
            m=(lo+hi)//2; c+=1
            if 2*m==t2: break
            if t2<2*m: hi=m-1
            else: lo=m+1
        best=max(best,c)
    return best
for n in range(1,300): assert worst(n)==n.bit_length()==math.floor(math.log2(n))+1
@lru_cache(None)
def C(n): return 0 if n==0 else 1+C(n//2)
for n in range(1,5001): assert C(n)==n.bit_length()
assert C(10**6)==20

from itertools import permutations

def ms(a,cnt):
    if len(a)<=1: return a
    h=(len(a)+1)//2; L=ms(a[:h],cnt); R=ms(a[h:],cnt); out=[];i=j=0
    while i<len(L) and j<len(R):
        cnt[0]+=1
        if L[i]<R[j]: out.append(L[i]); i+=1
        else: out.append(R[j]); j+=1
    return out+L[i:]+R[j:]
for n in range(1,8):

        c=[0]; assert ms(list(p),c)==sorted(p); w=max(w,c[0])
    assert w==M(n), (n,w,M(n))

# reviewer: optimal sorting of 5 items needs exactly 7 comparisons (minimax over consistent orders)
import itertools
from functools import lru_cache
perms=list(itertools.permutations(range(5)))
pairs=list(itertools.combinations(range(5),2))
@lru_cache(None)
def need(S):
    if len(S)<=1: return 0
    lo=(len(S)-1).bit_length()
    best=99
    for i,j in pairs:
        A=frozenset(p for p in S if p[i]<p[j]); B=S-A
        if not A or not B: continue
        if max(len(A),len(B))>2**(best-2) : continue
        v=1+max(need(A),need(B))
        if v<best: best=v
        if best==lo: break
    return best
assert need(frozenset(perms))==7

entry.sum: A finite automaton reads a string one symbol at a time, moving between finitely many states, and accepts or rejects the string according to the state it ends in. The languages recognised this way, the regular languages, are exactly those described by regular expressions; because the machine has only finite memory, languages such as $\{0^n1^n : n \ge 0\}$ are not regular, as the pumping lemma shows.
key: M = (Q, \Sigma, \delta, q_0, F), \quad L(M) = \{ w \in \Sigma^* : \delta^*(q_0, w) \in F \}
\text{DFA} \iff \text{NFA} \iff \text{regular expression} \quad \text{(Kleene's theorem, subset construction)}
L \text{ regular} \implies \exists p \ge 1\ \forall w \in L,\ |w| \ge p\ \exists x,y,z:\ w = xyz,\ |xy| \le p,\ |y| \ge 1,\ xy^iz \in L\ \forall i \ge 0
entry.why: Finite automata are the simplest model of a computer with bounded memory, and they are used directly in text search, lexical analysis in compilers, digital circuit design and protocol verification. They are also the first rung of the hierarchy of machine models that leads to Turing machines and the limits of computation.

links.note: Counting the strings of length $n$ accepted by an automaton reduces to powers of its transition matrix, so such counts always satisfy a linear recurrence and have rational generating functions.
Model checking represents system behaviours and specifications as automata and decides properties by product constructions and emptiness tests.
Each automaton generates a transition monoid, and the Myhill–Nerode theorem identifies the minimal automaton with the quotient of strings by an equivalence relation.

blocks.body:
A turnstile, a vending machine and the part of a compiler that splits code into words all do the same thing: they read input symbols one at a time and react according to a current state, of which there are only finitely many. A finite automaton is the mathematical model of such a device.

The model is simple enough that one can answer, with proof, exactly which tasks it can do. Can a machine with finite memory check whether a binary number is divisible by 3? Yes, with three states. Can it check whether a string of brackets is balanced? No, and the reason (it would have to count arbitrarily high) is made precise by the pumping lemma. Along the way, different-looking models turn out to have exactly the same power.

blocks.title: Strings and languages
blocks.body:
An alphabet $\Sigma$ is a finite nonempty set of symbols, for example $\{0, 1\}$ or $\{a, b\}$. A string (or word) over $\Sigma$ is a finite sequence of symbols; its length is written $|w|$, and the empty string, of length 0, is $\varepsilon$. The set of all strings is $\Sigma^*$. A language is any subset $L \subseteq \Sigma^*$ (see [[sets-relations]]).

Strings are joined by concatenation: if $x = 01$ and $y = 110$ then $xy = 01110$. For languages, $AB = \{xy : x \in A, y \in B\}$, and the star $A^* = \{\varepsilon\} \cup A \cup AA \cup AAA \cup \cdots$ is the set of all concatenations of finitely many strings from $A$. Write $y^i$ for $y$ repeated $i$ times, with $y^0 = \varepsilon$.

Examples of languages over $\{0,1\}$: all strings ending in 1; binary representations of multiples of 3; strings with no two consecutive 1s; $\{0^n 1^n : n \ge 0\}$. The question is which of these a finite machine can recognise.

blocks.title: Deterministic finite automaton
blocks.body:
A deterministic finite automaton (DFA) is a 5-tuple $M = (Q, \Sigma, \delta, q_0, F)$ where $Q$ is a finite set of states, $\Sigma$ an alphabet, $\delta : Q \times \Sigma \to Q$ the transition function, $q_0 \in Q$ the start state and $F \subseteq Q$ the set of accepting states.

Extend $\delta$ to strings recursively: $\delta^*(q, \varepsilon) = q$ and $\delta^*(q, wa) = \delta(\delta^*(q, w), a)$ for a string $w$ and symbol $a$. The language of $M$ is

$$L(M) = \{ w \in \Sigma^* : \delta^*(q_0, w) \in F \}.$$

A language is regular if some DFA recognises it. In words: start in $q_0$, follow one arrow per symbol, and accept if you finish in an accepting state.

blocks.title: Designing automata: remember only what matters
blocks.body:
The design question is always: what is the least information about the part of the string read so far that lets me finish the job? The states are exactly that information.

Multiples of 3 in binary. Reading a binary number from the left, if the part read so far has value $v$, appending a digit $a$ gives value $2v + a$. So whether the final number is divisible by 3 depends only on $v \bmod 3$, and that can be updated: the new remainder is $(2r + a) \bmod 3$. Take $Q = \{0, 1, 2\}$, $q_0 = 0$, $F = \{0\}$ and $\delta(r, a) = (2r + a) \bmod 3$. A proof that it works is an induction on the length of the input (see [[induction]]): $\delta^*(0, w)$ equals the value of $w$ modulo 3. The same idea gives an $m$-state DFA for multiples of any $m$, using [[congruences]].

No two consecutive 1s. Remember whether the last symbol was a 1, and whether a forbidden pair has already appeared: states "last was 0 or start" (A), "last was 1" (B) and "dead" (D). Transitions: from A, 0 goes to A and 1 to B; from B, 0 goes to A and 1 to D; D goes to D on both. Accepting states $\{A, B\}$.

Finite-state machines with output, such as a vending machine that emits a product or change, are the same idea with an output symbol attached to each transition (a Mealy machine) or to each state (a Moore machine). Recognising languages is the special case where the only output is accept or reject at the end.

blocks.title: Nondeterministic finite automaton
blocks.body:
A nondeterministic finite automaton (NFA) is like a DFA except that the transition function is $\delta : Q \times (\Sigma \cup \{\varepsilon\}) \to \mathcal{P}(Q)$: from a state, a symbol may lead to several states or none, and $\varepsilon$-moves change state without reading anything. An NFA accepts $w$ if at least one way of following the arrows while reading all of $w$ ends in an accepting state.

In words: the machine may guess, and it accepts if some lucky sequence of guesses works.

blocks.title: Subset construction
blocks.body: For every NFA $N$ with state set $Q$ there is a DFA $D$ with at most $2^{|Q|}$ states such that $L(D) = L(N)$. Hence NFAs recognise exactly the regular languages.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
For a set $S$ of states let $E(S)$ be the set of states reachable from $S$ by $\varepsilon$-moves alone (including $S$ itself). The states of $D$ are subsets of $Q$. Its start state is $E(\{q_0\})$, its transition is

$$\Delta(S, a) = E\Big(\bigcup_{q \in S} \delta(q, a)\Big),$$

and $S$ is accepting if $S$ contains an accepting state of $N$. By induction on $|w|$, $\Delta^*(E(\{q_0\}), w)$ is exactly the set of states $N$ can be in after reading $w$: true for $w = \varepsilon$ by definition, and the formula for $\Delta$ is precisely one step of "all possible moves". So $D$ accepts $w$ if and only if some run of $N$ on $w$ ends in an accepting state.

blocks.title: Regular expressions and Kleene's theorem
blocks.body:
Regular expressions build languages from single symbols using three operations: union ($R \mid S$), concatenation ($RS$) and star ($R^*$), together with $\varepsilon$ and the empty language $\emptyset$. For instance $(0 \mid 1)^*1$ describes strings ending in 1, and $(0 \mid 10)^*(\varepsilon \mid 1)$ describes strings with no two consecutive 1s: break the string after each 0, and every piece is 0 or 10, except possibly a final 1.

Kleene's theorem: a language is regular if and only if it is described by a regular expression. Proof sketch. From expression to automaton: build NFAs by induction on the expression; for a union, add a new start state with $\varepsilon$-moves to the two machines; for a concatenation, add $\varepsilon$-moves from the accepting states of the first to the start of the second; for a star, add a new accepting start state with an $\varepsilon$-move to the old start, and $\varepsilon$-moves from the old accepting states back to the old start. Then apply the subset construction. From automaton to expression: remove states one at a time, labelling arrows by regular expressions for the paths they replace, until only a start and an accepting state remain.

Closure properties follow cheaply. The complement of a regular language is regular: swap accepting and non-accepting states of a DFA. The intersection of two regular languages is regular: run both DFAs at once on pairs of states $(p, q)$, accepting when both components accept (the product construction). Union, concatenation and star come from Kleene's theorem.

blocks.title: Pumping lemma for regular languages
blocks.body:
If $L$ is regular, there is an integer $p \ge 1$ (a pumping length) such that every $w \in L$ with $|w| \ge p$ can be written $w = xyz$ with

1. $|xy| \le p$,
2. $|y| \ge 1$,
3. $xy^iz \in L$ for every $i \ge 0$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body: Let $M$ be a DFA for $L$ with $p$ states. Read $w = a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n$ with $n \ge p$ and list the states visited after $0, 1, \dots, p$ symbols: $s_0 = q_0, s_1, \dots, s_p$. These are $p + 1$ states from a set of size $p$, so by the [[pigeonhole]] principle $s_j = s_k$ for some $0 \le j < k \le p$. Let $x = a_1 \cdots a_j$, $y = a_{j+1} \cdots a_k$ and $z$ the rest. Then $|xy| = k \le p$ and $|y| = k - j \ge 1$. Reading $y$ takes the machine from $s_j$ back to the same state, so the loop can be traversed any number of times, including zero: $\delta^*(q_0, xy^iz) = \delta^*(q_0, xyz) \in F$ for every $i \ge 0$.

blocks.title: Tracing a run
blocks.body: Run the multiples-of-3 automaton on $w = 1101$ and on $w = 10010$. What do the results mean?
blocks.solution:
On $1101$: start in 0; reading 1 gives $(0 + 1) \bmod 3 = 1$; reading 1 gives $(2 + 1) \bmod 3 = 0$; reading 0 gives 0; reading 1 gives 1. The final state 1 is not accepting, so the string is rejected. Indeed $1101_2 = 13 = 3 \cdot 4 + 1$.

On $10010$: from 0, reading 1 gives 1; reading 0 gives $2 \bmod 3 = 2$; reading 0 gives $4 \bmod 3 = 1$; reading 1 gives $3 \bmod 3 = 0$; reading 0 gives 0. The run $0 \to 1 \to 2 \to 1 \to 0 \to 0$ ends in an accepting state, and indeed $10010_2 = 18 = 3 \cdot 6$. Tracing by hand is error-prone; the invariant "state = value of the prefix mod 3" is the reliable check.

blocks.title: From guessing to determinism
blocks.body: Let $L$ be the set of strings over $\{0,1\}$ whose second-to-last symbol is 1. Give a 3-state NFA for $L$, convert it to a DFA, and show that every DFA for $L$ needs at least 4 states.
blocks.solution:
NFA: state $a$ loops on 0 and 1; on reading 1 it may also guess "this is the second-to-last symbol" and move to $b$; from $b$ any symbol leads to $c$, which is accepting and has no outgoing arrows.

Subset construction from $\{a\}$: on 0 stay at $\{a\}$, on 1 go to $\{a, b\}$. From $\{a,b\}$: 0 gives $\{a, c\}$, 1 gives $\{a, b, c\}$. From $\{a, c\}$: 0 gives $\{a\}$, 1 gives $\{a, b\}$. From $\{a, b, c\}$: 0 gives $\{a, c\}$, 1 gives $\{a, b, c\}$. Four reachable subsets; the accepting ones are those containing $c$. In effect the DFA remembers the last two symbols read, counting missing symbols at the start as 0: $\{a\}$ means "00", $\{a,b\}$ means "01", $\{a,c\}$ means "10" and $\{a,b,c\}$ means "11".

Lower bound: take the four strings $00, 01, 10, 11$. For any two of them there is a suffix $z$ that sends one into $L$ and the other out. For example $10$ and $00$ differ on $z = \varepsilon$; $01$ and $00$ differ on $z = 0$ (giving $010 \in L$, $000 \notin L$); in general if two two-symbol strings differ in the first position use $z = \varepsilon$, and if they differ only in the second use $z = 0$. A DFA that sent two of them to the same state would treat them identically for every suffix. So the four strings reach four different states.

The same argument shows that "the $k$-th symbol from the end is 1" has a $(k+1)$-state NFA but needs $2^k$ states as a DFA: the exponential blow-up in the subset construction can really happen.

blocks.title: Not regular
blocks.body: Show that $L = \{0^n 1^n : n \ge 0\}$ is not regular. Deduce that the language of balanced bracket strings is not regular.
blocks.solution:
Suppose $L$ is regular with pumping length $p$. Take $w = 0^p 1^p \in L$. In any decomposition $w = xyz$ with $|xy| \le p$ and $|y| \ge 1$, the part $y$ lies inside the first $p$ symbols, so $y = 0^m$ with $m \ge 1$. Then $xy^2z = 0^{p+m}1^p$ has more 0s than 1s and is not in $L$, contradicting the lemma.

For brackets, write 0 for "(" and 1 for ")". If the balanced strings $B$ formed a regular language, then so would $B \cap 0^*1^*$, by the product construction, since $0^*1^*$ is regular. But a balanced string of the form $0^a1^b$ must have $a = b$, so $B \cap 0^*1^* = L$, which is not regular.

The idea: a finite machine cannot count without bound. After reading $0^n$ for $n$ larger than the number of states, two different counts land in the same state, and from then on the machine cannot tell them apart.

blocks.title: Counting accepted strings
blocks.body: How many binary strings of length 10 contain no two consecutive 1s?
blocks.solution:
Use the 3-state automaton A, B, D above. Let $A_n$ and $B_n$ be the numbers of strings of length $n$ that end in states A and B (strings ending in D are rejected). A string ends in A if its last symbol is 0 and it was in A or B before; it ends in B if the last symbol is 1 and it was in A before. So

$$A_n = A_{n-1} + B_{n-1}, \qquad B_n = A_{n-1},$$

with $A_0 = 1$, $B_0 = 0$. The total $t_n = A_n + B_n$ satisfies $t_n = t_{n-1} + t_{n-2}$, with $t_0 = 1$ and $t_1 = 2$, so $t_n = F_{n+2}$ (Fibonacci numbers with $F_1 = F_2 = 1$). For $n = 10$: $t_{10} = F_{12} = 144$.

The method is general: for any DFA, the number of accepted strings of length $n$ is $u^{\mathsf{T}} P^n v$, where $P_{st}$ counts the symbols leading from state $s$ to state $t$, $u$ marks the start state and $v$ the accepting states, so it satisfies a linear recurrence and has a rational [[generating-functions|generating function]].

blocks.body:
- The pumping lemma only goes one way. Every regular language satisfies it, but some non-regular languages satisfy it too, so it can prove non-regularity, never regularity.
- In a pumping argument you choose $w$ but not the decomposition: the contradiction must hold for every split $xyz$ with $|xy| \le p$ and $|y| \ge 1$.
- Finite languages are always regular, and infinite languages may well be regular: $(0 \mid 1)^*$ is infinite and recognised by one state.
- Nondeterminism does not add power to finite automata, but the equivalent DFA can be exponentially larger.
- A DFA must have a transition for every state and symbol. Diagrams often omit a dead state; remember it is there.

Regular languages are the bottom level of the Chomsky hierarchy. Adding a stack gives pushdown automata, which recognise the context-free languages (balanced brackets, most programming-language syntax). Adding an unbounded read-write tape gives Turing machines, the subject of [[computability]], where some questions about machines become undecidable; for DFAs, by contrast, almost everything is decidable: emptiness, equality of two languages and minimisation can all be computed. Automata also appear in logic (Büchi's theorem links them to monadic second-order logic, see [[logic-basics]]), in combinatorics on words, and in [[algorithms]] for pattern matching such as the Knuth–Morris–Pratt method.

1. Design a DFA over $\{0, 1\}$ accepting exactly the strings with an even number of 0s and an odd number of 1s. How many states are needed?
2. Write a regular expression for the strings over $\{a, b\}$ that contain $ab$ as a substring, and build a 3-state DFA for the same language.
3. Use the pumping lemma to show that $\{0^{n^2} : n \ge 0\}$ is not regular.
4. Show that if $L$ is regular then so is its reversal $\{a_n \cdots a_1 : a_1 \cdots a_n \in L\}$.

entry.sum: A Turing machine is a finite automaton equipped with an unbounded tape it can read, write and move along; by the Church–Turing thesis, it captures exactly what any algorithm can compute. Some well-posed problems have no algorithm at all: the halting problem, deciding whether a given machine halts on a given input, is undecidable, by a diagonal argument.
key: \mathrm{HALT} = \{ \langle M, w \rangle : M \text{ halts on input } w \} \text{ is recognisable but not decidable}
L \text{ decidable} \iff L \text{ and } \overline{L} \text{ are both recognisable}
\text{Rice: for every nontrivial property } P \text{ of recognisable languages, } \{\langle M \rangle : L(M) \text{ has } P\} \text{ is undecidable}
entry.why: Computability draws the outer boundary of what computers can ever do, independent of speed or memory: no program can reliably detect whether arbitrary programs loop forever, and problems as concrete as solving Diophantine equations in integers turn out to have no general algorithm. The same diagonal idea underlies Gödel's incompleteness theorems.

links.note: The Matiyasevich–Robinson–Davis–Putnam theorem shows that no algorithm decides whether a polynomial equation with integer coefficients has an integer solution, answering Hilbert's tenth problem negatively.
The Novikov–Boone theorem gives a finitely presented group whose word problem, deciding whether a word in the generators equals the identity, is undecidable.
Rice's theorem explains why program verifiers must either restrict the programs they accept, require human-supplied proofs, or sometimes answer 'unknown'.

blocks.body:
In 1900 Hilbert asked for a procedure that decides, for any polynomial equation with integer coefficients, whether it has an integer solution. To prove that no such procedure exists, one first needs a precise definition of "procedure". In 1936 Turing gave one: a machine so simple it can be described in a paragraph, yet, as far as anyone has ever found, able to carry out any algorithm at all.

With that definition one can prove impossibility results. The most famous is that no program can decide, for every program and input, whether that program eventually stops. This page builds the model from [[automata|finite automata]], proves the halting problem undecidable, and shows how that one result spreads to many others.

blocks.title: From finite automata to Turing machines
blocks.body:
A finite automaton reads its input once, left to right, and has no memory beyond its current state. That is why it cannot recognise $\{0^n1^n\}$: it cannot count. Give it a tape instead: an infinite row of cells, each holding a symbol, with the input written at the start and blanks everywhere else. The machine has a head over one cell. In each step it reads the symbol under the head and, depending on that symbol and its current state, writes a symbol, moves one cell left or right, and changes state. It stops when it enters a special accept or reject state. It may also never stop.

That is the whole model. Its power comes from the unbounded tape, which serves as scratch paper of unlimited size.

blocks.title: Turing machine
blocks.body:
A Turing machine is a tuple $M = (Q, \Sigma, \Gamma, \delta, q_0, q_{\mathrm{acc}}, q_{\mathrm{rej}})$ where $Q$ is a finite set of states, $\Sigma$ the input alphabet, $\Gamma \supseteq \Sigma \cup \{\sqcup\}$ the tape alphabet with blank symbol $\sqcup \notin \Sigma$, $q_0$ the start state, $q_{\mathrm{acc}} \ne q_{\mathrm{rej}}$ the halting states, and

$$\delta : (Q \setminus \{q_{\mathrm{acc}}, q_{\mathrm{rej}}\}) \times \Gamma \to Q \times \Gamma \times \{L, R\}$$

the transition function. On input $w \in \Sigma^*$ the tape starts as $w$ followed by blanks, with the head on the first cell and state $q_0$. $M$ accepts $w$ if the computation reaches $q_{\mathrm{acc}}$, rejects $w$ if it reaches $q_{\mathrm{rej}}$, and loops otherwise.

A language $L$ is recognisable (also called recursively enumerable) if some $M$ accepts exactly the strings in $L$; on other strings it may reject or loop. $L$ is decidable (recursive) if some $M$ accepts every string in $L$ and rejects every string outside $L$, so it always halts.

blocks.title: The Church–Turing thesis and the universal machine
blocks.body:
Many variations of the model have been proposed: several tapes, a two-dimensional tape, nondeterministic choices, random-access memory. Each can be simulated by an ordinary Turing machine, often with only a polynomial slowdown. Completely different definitions of computable function from the 1930s, Church's lambda calculus and Gödel–Kleene recursive functions, define exactly the same class. The Church–Turing thesis is the claim that this class is exactly what is computable by any effective procedure. It is not a theorem, because "effective procedure" is informal, but it is so well supported that "algorithm" and "Turing machine" are used interchangeably.

A Turing machine is a finite object, so it can be written as a string $\langle M \rangle$: list the transitions in some fixed format. Turing showed that there is a universal machine $U$ which, given $\langle M, w \rangle$, simulates $M$ on $w$ step by step, accepting if $M$ accepts and rejecting if $M$ rejects. This is the theoretical ancestor of the stored-program computer: one machine, many programs, programs as data. It also shows at once that

$$\mathrm{HALT} = \{\langle M, w\rangle : M \text{ halts on } w\}$$

is recognisable: simulate, and accept if the simulation ever halts.

blocks.title: Adding one in binary
blocks.body: Design a Turing machine that, given a binary number on the tape, replaces it by the number plus 1, and trace it on 1011.
blocks.solution:
Two working states. State $r$ ("go right"): on 0 or 1, leave it and move right; on a blank, move left and switch to state $c$ ("carry"). State $c$: on 1, write 0 and move left, staying in $c$; on 0 or blank, write 1 and halt.

(Strictly, the definition above has the head start at the left end and only allows moving off the left end if the tape is two-way infinite; take the tape to be infinite in both directions here, which does not change what can be computed.)

Trace on 1011: in state $r$ the head runs right past 1, 0, 1, 1, reaches the blank, steps back onto the last 1 and enters $c$. The carry turns the last 1 into 0, moves left, turns the next 1 into 0, moves left onto the 0, writes 1 and halts. The tape reads 1100, and indeed $1011_2 + 1 = 11 + 1 = 12 = 1100_2$. On 111 the carry runs off the left end onto a blank and writes 1 there, giving 1000.

A machine that halts with an answer on its tape computes a function; this is the sense in which Turing machines compute functions as well as recognise languages.

blocks.title: Recognising 0^n 1^n
blocks.body: Describe a Turing machine that decides $\{0^n1^n : n \ge 0\}$, which no finite automaton can recognise, and estimate how many steps it takes.
blocks.solution:
Use two extra tape symbols $X$ and $Y$ to cross off matched symbols. Repeat: at the leftmost unmarked symbol, if it is a 0, overwrite it with $X$, move right past 0s and $Y$s to the first 1, overwrite it with $Y$, and move back left to the rightmost $X$; then step right and repeat. If instead a 1 is found where a 0 was expected, or no 1 is found when one is needed, reject. When no 0s remain, scan right over the $Y$s: accept if the next symbol is a blank, reject if it is anything else.

Each round crosses off one 0 and one 1, so the machine halts on every input and accepts exactly when the numbers match and all 0s come first. Each round walks across the string and back, about $2n$ steps, and there are $n$ rounds, so on $0^n1^n$ the running time grows like $2n^2$. The finite automaton could not count; the Turing machine counts by writing on its tape.

blocks.title: Decidable means recognisable from both sides
blocks.body: A language $L$ is decidable if and only if both $L$ and its complement $\overline{L}$ are recognisable.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
If $M$ decides $L$, then $M$ recognises $L$, and $M$ with its accept and reject states swapped recognises $\overline{L}$.

Conversely, let $M_1$ recognise $L$ and $M_2$ recognise $\overline{L}$. On input $w$, simulate $M_1$ and $M_2$ alternately, one step each. Every $w$ lies in $L$ or in $\overline{L}$, so one of the two simulations eventually accepts. If $M_1$ accepts, accept; if $M_2$ accepts, reject. This always halts and gives the right answer. Note that running $M_1$ to completion first would not work, since it may loop on $w \notin L$.

blocks.title: The halting problem is undecidable
blocks.body: There is no Turing machine that, given $\langle M, w\rangle$, always halts and accepts exactly when $M$ halts on $w$. Consequently the complement of $\mathrm{HALT}$ is not recognisable.

blocks.title: Proof (diagonal argument)
blocks.body:
Suppose $H$ decides $\mathrm{HALT}$. Build a machine $D$ that, on input $\langle M\rangle$, runs $H$ on $\langle M, \langle M\rangle\rangle$, asking whether $M$ halts when fed its own description, and then does the opposite: if $H$ says "halts", $D$ enters an infinite loop; if $H$ says "does not halt", $D$ halts.

Now run $D$ on $\langle D\rangle$. If $D$ halts on $\langle D\rangle$, then $H$ said "halts", so $D$ loops: contradiction. If $D$ does not halt on $\langle D\rangle$, then $H$ said "does not halt", so $D$ halts: contradiction. Hence $H$ cannot exist.

Since $\mathrm{HALT}$ is recognisable but not decidable, the previous theorem shows $\overline{\mathrm{HALT}}$ is not recognisable.

The structure is Cantor's diagonal argument (see [[ordinals-cardinals]]): list all machines as rows and all inputs as columns, and build a machine that differs from row $i$ at column $i$. A counting version of the same idea: there are only countably many machines, since each is a finite string, but uncountably many languages over $\{0,1\}$, so most languages are not even recognisable.

blocks.title: Reductions and Rice's theorem
blocks.body:
Once one problem is known to be undecidable, others follow by reduction: show that a decider for the new problem $B$ could be used to build a decider for $\mathrm{HALT}$. Then $B$ must be undecidable too.

For example, let $$E = \{\langle M\rangle : M \text{ halts when started on a blank tape}\}$$. Given $\langle M, w\rangle$, construct the machine $M_w$ that first writes $w$ on its blank tape and then behaves like $M$. Then $M_w$ halts on a blank tape exactly when $M$ halts on $w$. The map $\langle M, w\rangle \mapsto \langle M_w\rangle$ is computable, so a decider for $E$ would decide $\mathrm{HALT}$. Hence $E$ is undecidable.

Generalising this trick gives Rice's theorem: let $P$ be any property of recognisable languages that some recognisable language has and some does not. Then $\{\langle M\rangle : L(M) \text{ has property } P\}$ is undecidable. So "does this program accept every input?", "does it accept the string 0?", "is its language regular?" are all undecidable. Rice's theorem is about the language a machine recognises, not about the machine's code: "does $M$ have at most 10 states?" is decidable by inspection.

Undecidability is not only about machines. By Matiyasevich's theorem (1970), completing earlier work of Davis, Putnam and Robinson, every recognisable set of natural numbers is the set of values of a parameter for which some polynomial equation has a solution in natural numbers; so no algorithm decides solvability of [[diophantine]] equations, which settles Hilbert's tenth problem. The word problem for finitely presented [[groups]] is also undecidable (Novikov and Boone).

blocks.title: The busy beaver
blocks.body: Among all Turing machines with $n$ working states, tape alphabet $\{0, 1\}$, started on a blank (all-0) tape, let $S(n)$ be the largest number of steps taken by one that eventually halts. Show that $S$ is not computable.
blocks.solution:
Count a step as one transition, including the final move into the halting state. There are only finitely many machines with $n$ states, so $S(n)$ is a well-defined number. Suppose some algorithm computed $S(n)$ from $n$. Then we could decide whether a given $n$-state machine $M$ halts on a blank tape: compute $S(n)$, run $M$ for $S(n)$ steps, and answer "halts" if it has halted by then and "never halts" otherwise. This is correct because any $n$-state machine that halts at all does so within $S(n)$ steps. That would decide the undecidable problem $E$ above (restricted to two tape symbols, which is still undecidable), a contradiction.

Small values are known. The 2-state champion (A on 0: write 1, move right, go to B; A on 1: write 1, move left, go to B; B on 0: write 1, move left, go to A; B on 1: write 1, move right, halt) halts after 6 steps leaving four 1s, and $S(2) = 6$. Known values are $S(3) = 21$ and $S(4) = 107$, and in 2024 a collaborative, computer-verified proof established $S(5) = 47{,}176{,}870$. In fact $S$ eventually grows faster than every computable function.

blocks.body:
- Undecidable does not mean that no instance can be solved. For particular machines one can often prove halting or looping; what fails is a single algorithm that works for every machine.
- Undecidability is not about being slow. A decidable problem can take astronomically long; an undecidable one has no algorithm at any speed.
- Recognisable is weaker than decidable. A recogniser may run forever on strings outside the language, and you cannot in general tell "still running" from "will never stop".
- The Church–Turing thesis is a claim about the informal notion of algorithm. It is not proved, and it says nothing about efficiency.
- The halting problem is undecidable for Turing machines, but it is decidable for finite automata and for any machine with a fixed bounded amount of memory, since such a machine has finitely many configurations and must repeat one if it runs too long.

The diagonal argument here reappears in logic as Gödel's [[incompleteness]] theorems: the set of theorems of a consistent, effectively axiomatised theory of arithmetic is recognisable, and if it contained every true statement about whether machines halt, the halting problem would become decidable. Restricting attention to decidable problems and asking how many steps they need leads to complexity theory and the [[p-vs-np]] question; see also [[algorithms]]. The model of computation with finite memory is studied on [[automata]], and the link with formal proofs continues in [[logic-basics]] and [[completeness-theorem]].

1. Design a Turing machine that decides whether a binary string is a palindrome, and estimate its running time.
2. Show that the decidable languages are closed under union, intersection and complement, and that the recognisable languages are closed under union and intersection.
3. Show by a reduction from the halting problem that it is undecidable whether two Turing machines recognise the same language.
4. Why does the proof that the halting problem is undecidable fail if you apply it to finite automata instead of Turing machines?

Boolos, Burgess & Jeffrey, Computability and Logic
Rosen, Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications, 6th ed.

entry.sum: A quadratic function $f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c$ with $a \ne 0$ has a parabola as its graph, with vertex at $x = -\tfrac{b}{2a}$. Completing the square turns any quadratic into the form $a(x-h)^2 + k$, from which the quadratic formula, the maximum or minimum value, and the number of real roots (decided by the discriminant $b^2 - 4ac$) all follow.
key: ax^2 + bx + c = 0,\ a \ne 0 \iff x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}
ax^2 + bx + c = a\left(x + \frac{b}{2a}\right)^2 - \frac{b^2 - 4ac}{4a}
\Delta = b^2 - 4ac:\quad \Delta > 0 \text{ two real roots},\ \Delta = 0 \text{ one repeated root},\ \Delta < 0 \text{ no real roots}
entry.why: Quadratics are the first nonlinear functions everyone meets, and they model projectile heights, areas, and profits that rise and then fall. The discriminant trick, that a quadratic which is never negative cannot have two distinct real roots, proves inequalities as strong as Cauchy–Schwarz.

links.note: Under constant gravity the height of a projectile is a quadratic function of time, so its maximum height and landing time come from the vertex and the roots.
Minimising a quadratic by completing the square is the one-variable case of least-squares and quadratic programming, where the minimum of a convex quadratic is found exactly.
Intersecting a line with a circle or a parabola leads to a quadratic equation, and the sign of its discriminant says whether the line misses, touches or cuts the curve.

refs: Gelfand & Shen, Algebra
Rusczyk, Introduction to Algebra
Stewart, Redlin & Watson, Precalculus: Mathematics for Calculus

blocks.body:
A farmer has 60 metres of fencing and wants a rectangular pen against a long wall. If the two sides perpendicular to the wall each have length $x$, the area is $x(60 - 2x)$. Which $x$ gives the most area? A ball is thrown upward and its height after $t$ seconds is $20t - 5t^2$ metres. When does it land, and how high does it go?

Both questions are about expressions of the form $ax^2 + bx + c$. This page shows how one algebraic move, completing the square, answers every basic question about them: where the graph turns, what its highest or lowest value is, and where it crosses the axis.

blocks.title: The shape of a quadratic
blocks.body:
Start with $y = x^2$. A small table: at $x = -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3$ the values are $9, 4, 1, 0, 1, 4, 9$. The graph is a U-shaped curve, a parabola, symmetric about the line $x = 0$, with its lowest point, the vertex, at the origin.

Every other quadratic graph is this one moved and stretched (see [[functions]] for how such transformations act on graphs). The graph of $y = a(x - h)^2 + k$ is $y = x^2$ stretched vertically by the factor $a$ (and flipped if $a < 0$), then shifted so that the vertex is at $(h, k)$. Its axis of symmetry is the line $x = h$. If $a > 0$ it opens upward and $k$ is the minimum value; if $a < 0$ it opens downward and $k$ is the maximum.

So if we can rewrite $ax^2 + bx + c$ in this vertex form, we can read off everything.

blocks.title: Quadratic function
blocks.body:
A quadratic function is a function $f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c$ with real constants $a, b, c$ and $a \ne 0$. A root (or zero) of $f$ is a number $r$ with $f(r) = 0$; the roots of $f$ are the solutions of the quadratic equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ and, when real, the $x$-coordinates where the graph meets the $x$-axis. The number $\Delta = b^2 - 4ac$ is the discriminant.

The condition $a \ne 0$ matters: without it the expression is linear and its graph is a line.

blocks.title: Completing the square
blocks.body:
The identity $(x + p)^2 = x^2 + 2px + p^2$ says that $x^2 + 2px$ is a perfect square except for the missing $p^2$. Take $x^2 + 6x + 5$. Here $2p = 6$, so $p = 3$, and

$$x^2 + 6x + 5 = (x^2 + 6x + 9) - 9 + 5 = (x + 3)^2 - 4.$$

Now the graph is visible: vertex $(-3, -4)$, opening upward, minimum value $-4$. The roots satisfy $(x+3)^2 = 4$, so $x + 3 = \pm 2$ and $x = -1$ or $x = -5$. Note that the vertex lies halfway between the roots, as symmetry demands.

With a leading coefficient, factor it out first: $$2x^2 - 12x + 7 = 2(x^2 - 6x) + 7 = 2\big((x - 3)^2 - 9\big) + 7 = 2(x - 3)^2 - 11$$.

Doing the same with letters, for $a \ne 0$:

$$ax^2 + bx + c = a\left(x^2 + \frac{b}{a}x\right) + c = a\left(x + \frac{b}{2a}\right)^2 - \frac{b^2}{4a} + c = a\left(x + \frac{b}{2a}\right)^2 - \frac{b^2 - 4ac}{4a}.$$

So the vertex is at $x = -\frac{b}{2a}$, with value $-\frac{\Delta}{4a}$.

blocks.title: The quadratic formula
blocks.body:
Let $a, b, c$ be real with $a \ne 0$, and $\Delta = b^2 - 4ac$.

1. If $\Delta > 0$, the equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ has exactly two real solutions, $x = \dfrac{-b + \sqrt{\Delta}}{2a}$ and $x = \dfrac{-b - \sqrt{\Delta}}{2a}$.
2. If $\Delta = 0$, it has exactly one real solution, $x = -\dfrac{b}{2a}$ (a repeated root).
3. If $\Delta < 0$, it has no real solutions.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
By completing the square, the equation is equivalent to

$$a\left(x + \frac{b}{2a}\right)^2 = \frac{\Delta}{4a}, \quad\text{that is,}\quad \left(x + \frac{b}{2a}\right)^2 = \frac{\Delta}{4a^2}.$$

The right side has the sign of $\Delta$, since $4a^2 > 0$. A square is never negative, so if $\Delta < 0$ there is no solution. If $\Delta = 0$, the square is zero exactly when $x = -\frac{b}{2a}$. If $\Delta > 0$, a number squares to $\frac{\Delta}{4a^2}$ exactly when it equals $\pm\frac{\sqrt{\Delta}}{2|a|}$, and as $\pm$ covers both signs this is the same as $\pm\frac{\sqrt{\Delta}}{2a}$. So $x = -\frac{b}{2a} \pm \frac{\sqrt{\Delta}}{2a}$, two different numbers because $\sqrt{\Delta} \ne 0$.

blocks.title: Factorised form and Vieta's formulas
blocks.body:
If $r$ and $s$ are the roots (equal when $\Delta = 0$), then

$$ax^2 + bx + c = a(x - r)(x - s).$$

To see it, expand the right side: $a x^2 - a(r+s)x + ars$. With the formula, $r + s = -\frac{b}{a}$ (the square roots cancel) and $rs = \frac{b^2 - \Delta}{4a^2} = \frac{4ac}{4a^2} = \frac{c}{a}$. Comparing coefficients gives Vieta's formulas,

$$r + s = -\frac{b}{a}, \qquad rs = \frac{c}{a},$$

which are the two-root case of the general relations on [[polynomials-roots]]. They let you work with the roots without finding them, and they explain factorising by inspection: to factor $x^2 - 7x + 12$, look for two numbers with sum 7 and product 12, namely 3 and 4, so $x^2 - 7x + 12 = (x-3)(x-4)$.

Three pictures of the same quadratic are now available: standard form $ax^2 + bx + c$ (shows the $y$-intercept $c$), vertex form (shows the turning point) and factorised form (shows the roots). Moving between them is most of the craft.

blocks.title: The fence and the ball
blocks.body: (a) Maximise the area $A(x) = x(60 - 2x)$ of the pen from the introduction. (b) A ball's height is $h(t) = 20t - 5t^2$ metres. Find its maximum height and when it lands.
blocks.solution:
(a) $A(x) = -2x^2 + 60x = -2(x^2 - 30x) = -2(x - 15)^2 + 450$. Since $-2(x - 15)^2 \le 0$, the area is at most 450, with equality at $x = 15$. The pen is 15 m by 30 m, with the long side along the wall.

(b) $h(t) = -5(t^2 - 4t) = -5(t - 2)^2 + 20$. The maximum height is 20 m, at $t = 2$ s. It lands when $h(t) = 0$, that is $5t(4 - t) = 0$, so at $t = 4$ s (the root $t = 0$ is the moment of throwing). The peak is halfway between the two roots, as the symmetry of the parabola predicts.

blocks.title: Touching a parabola
blocks.body: For which values of $k$ does the line $y = kx - 1$ touch the parabola $y = x^2 + 3$ at exactly one point? Find the point of contact.
blocks.solution:
Points on both graphs satisfy $x^2 + 3 = kx - 1$, that is $x^2 - kx + 4 = 0$. The line meets the parabola once exactly when this has one (repeated) solution, so when the discriminant is zero: $k^2 - 16 = 0$, so $k = 4$ or $k = -4$.

The repeated root is $x = \frac{k}{2}$. For $k = 4$ the contact point is $(2, 7)$; for $k = -4$ it is $(-2, 7)$. For $|k| > 4$ the line cuts the parabola twice, and for $|k| < 4$ it misses it. The discriminant turns a geometric question into an arithmetic one.

blocks.title: Using the roots without finding them
blocks.body: Let $r, s$ be the roots of $x^2 - 5x + 3 = 0$. Find $r^2 + s^2$, $\frac1r + \frac1s$ and $r^3 + s^3$, and write down a quadratic equation whose roots are $r^2$ and $s^2$.
blocks.solution:
By Vieta, $r + s = 5$ and $rs = 3$.

$r^2 + s^2 = (r + s)^2 - 2rs = 25 - 6 = 19$.

$\frac1r + \frac1s = \frac{r + s}{rs} = \frac53$.

$r^3 + s^3 = (r+s)^3 - 3rs(r+s) = 125 - 45 = 80$.

The numbers $r^2, s^2$ have sum 19 and product $(rs)^2 = 9$, so they are the roots of $x^2 - 19x + 9 = 0$.

As a check, the roots are $\frac{5 \pm \sqrt{13}}{2}$, and $\left(\frac{5 + \sqrt{13}}{2}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{5 - \sqrt{13}}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{2(25 + 13)}{4} = 19$.

blocks.title: One equation, two unknowns
blocks.body: Find all real pairs $(x, y)$ with $x^2 + xy + y^2 - 3x - 3y + 3 = 0$.
blocks.solution:
One equation in two unknowns usually has infinitely many solutions, but here think of it as a quadratic in $x$ with $y$ fixed:

$$x^2 + (y - 3)x + (y^2 - 3y + 3) = 0.$$

For a real $x$ to exist, the discriminant must be at least zero:

$$\Delta = (y - 3)^2 - 4(y^2 - 3y + 3) = -3y^2 + 6y - 3 = -3(y - 1)^2 \ge 0.$$

This forces $y = 1$. Then the equation is $x^2 - 2x + 1 = (x - 1)^2 = 0$, so $x = 1$. The only solution is $(1, 1)$.

The curve described by the equation is an ellipse that has shrunk to a single point. Treating a two-variable equation as a quadratic in one variable and demanding a non-negative discriminant is a standard competition technique.

blocks.title: Further: complex roots and the discriminant trick
blocks.body:
When $\Delta < 0$ the formula still makes sense with [[complex-numbers]]: $x^2 + 2x + 5 = 0$ gives $x = \frac{-2 \pm \sqrt{-16}}{2} = -1 \pm 2i$. Over the complex numbers every quadratic has two roots counted with multiplicity, and they are complex conjugates when the coefficients are real. Vieta's formulas still hold: $(-1 + 2i) + (-1 - 2i) = -2$ and $(-1+2i)(-1-2i) = 5$.

The discriminant is also a tool for proving inequalities. If a quadratic $q(t) = At^2 + Bt + C$ with $A > 0$ satisfies $q(t) \ge 0$ for every real $t$, then it cannot have two distinct real roots (it would be negative between them), so $B^2 - 4AC \le 0$. Apply this to

$$q(t) = (a_1 t + b_1)^2 + (a_2 t + b_2)^2 + \cdots + (a_n t + b_n)^2,$$

which is a sum of squares and so never negative. Expanding, $A = \sum a_i^2$, $B = 2\sum a_i b_i$, $C = \sum b_i^2$, and $B^2 \le 4AC$ becomes

$$\Big(\sum a_i b_i\Big)^2 \le \Big(\sum a_i^2\Big)\Big(\sum b_i^2\Big),$$

the [[cauchy-schwarz]] inequality (if all $a_i = 0$ it is trivial). The same idea, applied to $\langle u + tv, u + tv \rangle \ge 0$, proves it in any real [[inner-products|inner product space]].

Finally, the same algebra works in other number systems: the formula solves $ax^2 + bx + c \equiv 0 \pmod p$ for an odd prime $p$ with $p \nmid a$ exactly when $\Delta$ has a square root modulo $p$, which is the subject of [[quadratic-residues]].

- Dividing both sides of $x^2 = 3x$ by $x$ loses the root $x = 0$. Instead write $x(x - 3) = 0$.
- The vertex is at $x = -\frac{b}{2a}$, not $\frac{b}{2a}$. For $x^2 + 6x + 5$ it is at $x = -3$.
- When completing the square with $a \ne 1$, factor $a$ out first, and remember that the constant you add inside the bracket is multiplied by $a$.
- From $(x - 2)^2 = 9$ the conclusion is $x - 2 = \pm 3$, not only $x - 2 = 3$.
- $\Delta < 0$ means no real roots; it does not mean the equation is wrong, and over $\mathbb{C}$ there are two roots.
- An expression like $kx^2 + 2x + 1$ is only quadratic when $k \ne 0$; questions with a parameter need the case $k = 0$ checked separately.

Knowing where a quadratic is positive or negative is the starting point for [[solving-inequalities]]. Parabolas are one of the [[conic-sections]], and the discriminant $B^2 - 4AC$ of a general second-degree equation $Ax^2 + Bxy + Cy^2 + \dots = 0$ decides whether a non-degenerate curve of this kind is an ellipse, parabola or hyperbola. Higher-degree equations and the full form of Vieta's formulas are on [[polynomials-roots]]; two-variable quadratic expressions $ax^2 + bxy + cy^2$ in number theory are on [[quadratic-forms]]. In calculus, the vertex is where the derivative $2ax + b$ vanishes (see [[derivative]]).

1. Write $3x^2 + 12x - 1$ in vertex form, and state its minimum value and axis of symmetry.
2. Find all values of $m$ for which $x^2 + mx + 9 = 0$ has a repeated root, and find the root in each case.
3. The roots of $2x^2 - 3x - 7 = 0$ are $r$ and $s$. Find $(r - s)^2$ without solving the equation.
4. Show that $x^2 + y^2 + 1 \ge xy + x + y$ for all real $x, y$, with equality only at $x = y = 1$, by treating the difference as a quadratic in $x$.

entry.sum: Solving an inequality means finding the set of all values that make it true, usually a union of intervals. The key rules are that adding anything preserves an inequality while multiplying by a negative number reverses it; polynomial and rational inequalities are solved by finding where each factor changes sign and reading off a sign chart, never by multiplying through by an expression of unknown sign.
key: a < b \text{ and } c < 0 \implies ac > bc
a > 0,\ r < s:\quad a(x - r)(x - s) < 0 \iff r < x < s
|x - a| < d \iff a - d < x < a + d \quad (d > 0)
entry.why: Inequalities describe constraints: budgets, tolerances, safe ranges of a dose, feasible production plans. Solving them exactly, including the sign-chart method for rational expressions, is the everyday tool behind estimates in analysis and the feasible regions of linear programming.

links.note: A system of linear inequalities in several variables defines a convex feasible region, and linear programming optimises a linear objective over it.
Limit and continuity proofs consist of solving inequalities such as $|x - a| < \delta$ to guarantee $|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon$.

blocks.body:
An equation such as $x^2 = 4$ usually has a few solutions. An inequality such as $x^2 < 4$ usually has infinitely many, here every number strictly between $-2$ and $2$. Solving an inequality means describing that whole set exactly, usually as an interval or a union of intervals.

The algebra looks like equation solving, with two traps: multiplying by a negative number reverses the inequality, and multiplying by an expression whose sign you do not know is not allowed at all. This page gives the rules, the sign-chart method that handles polynomial and rational inequalities, and the tricks for absolute values and square roots.

blocks.title: Notation and the basic rules
blocks.body:
Interval notation: $(a, b)$ is the set of $x$ with $a < x < b$; a square bracket includes the endpoint, so $[a, b)$ means $a \le x < b$; $(-\infty, b]$ means $x \le b$. The symbol $\cup$ joins sets: $(-\infty, -1) \cup (3, \infty)$ is "less than $-1$ or greater than 3".

Everything rests on one idea: $a < b$ means that $b - a$ is positive, and positive numbers are closed under addition and multiplication. From this:

1. If $a < b$, then $a + c < b + c$ for every $c$, because $(b + c) - (a + c) = b - a$.
2. If $a < b$ and $c > 0$, then $ac < bc$, because $bc - ac = (b - a)c$ is a product of positives.
3. If $a < b$ and $c < 0$, then $ac > bc$, because $ac - bc = (b - a)(-c)$ is a product of positives.
4. If $0 \le a < b$, then $a^2 < b^2$, because $b^2 - a^2 = (b - a)(b + a)$ with both factors positive. Squaring needs both sides non-negative: $-3 < 2$ but $9 > 4$.

Example: $-2x + 5 > 11$ gives $-2x > 6$, and dividing by $-2$ reverses the sign: $x < -3$. A compound inequality is handled in one go: $-3 < 2x + 1 \le 7$ gives $-4 < 2x \le 6$, so $-2 < x \le 3$, that is, $x \in (-2, 3]$.

blocks.title: Quadratic inequalities
blocks.body:
The graph of a quadratic tells you where it is positive (see [[quadratics]]). Take $x^2 - x - 6 = (x + 2)(x - 3)$. Its parabola opens upward and crosses the axis at $-2$ and $3$, so it is below the axis between the roots and above it outside. Hence

$$x^2 - x - 6 < 0 \iff -2 < x < 3, \qquad x^2 - x - 6 \ge 0 \iff x \le -2 \text{ or } x \ge 3.$$

A quick table confirms it: at $x = -3, 0, 4$ the values are $6, -6, 6$.

If the discriminant is negative the parabola never meets the axis, so the quadratic has the same sign as $a$ for every $x$. For example $x^2 + 2x + 5 = (x + 1)^2 + 4 > 0$ always, so $x^2 + 2x + 5 < 0$ has no solutions and $x^2 + 2x + 5 > 0$ holds for all real $x$.

blocks.title: Sign of a quadratic
blocks.body:
Let $f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c$ with $a \ne 0$ and $\Delta = b^2 - 4ac$.

1. If $\Delta > 0$ and the roots are $r < s$, then $f(x)$ has the sign of $-a$ for $r < x < s$, and the sign of $a$ for $x < r$ and for $x > s$.
2. If $\Delta = 0$ with repeated root $r$, then $f(x)$ has the sign of $a$ for every $x \ne r$.
3. If $\Delta < 0$, then $f(x)$ has the sign of $a$ for every real $x$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body: In case 1, $f(x) = a(x - r)(x - s)$. For $r < x < s$ the factor $x - r$ is positive and $x - s$ is negative, so the product $(x-r)(x-s)$ is negative; outside $[r, s]$ both factors have the same sign, so it is positive. Multiplying by $a$ gives the claim. In case 2, $f(x) = a(x - r)^2$, and $(x - r)^2 > 0$ for $x \ne r$. In case 3, completing the square gives $f(x) = a\left[\left(x + \frac{b}{2a}\right)^2 + \frac{-\Delta}{4a^2}\right]$, and the bracket is positive since $-\Delta > 0$.

blocks.title: Sign charts for products and quotients
blocks.body:
The proof above generalises. A product of linear factors can only change sign where one of its factors is zero, so:

1. Move everything to one side, so the inequality compares a single expression with 0.
2. Factor it completely, numerator and denominator.
3. Mark the zeros of every factor on the number line. They split it into intervals.
4. On each interval, every factor has a constant sign; count the negative factors (or test one point) to find the sign of the whole expression.
5. Read off the intervals with the required sign. Include zeros of the numerator for $\le$ or $\ge$, and never include zeros of the denominator.

For $(x - 1)(x + 2)(x - 4) > 0$, the critical points are $-2, 1, 4$. For $x > 4$ all three factors are positive, and each time $x$ passes a critical point going left, exactly one factor changes sign. So the signs on $(-\infty, -2)$, $(-2, 1)$, $(1, 4)$, $(4, \infty)$ are $-, +, -, +$, and the solution is $(-2, 1) \cup (4, \infty)$.

A squared factor such as $(x - 3)^2$ does not change sign at $x = 3$; only factors raised to odd powers do.

For rational inequalities the crucial rule is: do not multiply both sides by a denominator unless you know its sign. Subtract instead and combine into one fraction, as in the next example. (One may also multiply by the square of the denominator, which is positive, but the fraction method is cleaner.)

blocks.title: A rational inequality
blocks.body: Solve $\dfrac{x + 1}{x - 2} \le 2$.
blocks.solution:
Multiplying by $x - 2$ would be wrong, since $x - 2$ is negative for $x < 2$. Instead,

$$\frac{x + 1}{x - 2} - 2 = \frac{x + 1 - 2(x - 2)}{x - 2} = \frac{5 - x}{x - 2} \le 0, \quad\text{equivalently}\quad \frac{x - 5}{x - 2} \ge 0.$$

Critical points: $x = 2$ (excluded, the expression is undefined) and $x = 5$ (included, the expression is 0). Signs of $\frac{x-5}{x-2}$ on $(-\infty, 2)$, $(2, 5)$, $(5, \infty)$: $+, -, +$. Solution: $(-\infty, 2) \cup [5, \infty)$.

Check: $x = 0$ gives $-\frac12 \le 2$, true; $x = 3$ gives $4 \le 2$, false; $x = 5$ gives $2 \le 2$, true; $x = 6$ gives $\frac74 \le 2$, true. Had we multiplied through by $x - 2$, we would have found $x \ge 5$ only and lost all of $(-\infty, 2)$.

blocks.title: Absolute values and square roots
blocks.body:
The absolute value $|x - a|$ is the distance between $x$ and $a$ on the number line. So for $d > 0$:

$$|x - a| < d \iff a - d < x < a + d, \qquad |x - a| > d \iff x < a - d \text{ or } x > a + d.$$

For example $|2x - 3| < 5$ means $-5 < 2x - 3 < 5$, so $-1 < x < 4$. When both sides involve $x$, or there are several absolute values, split into cases according to the sign of each expression inside.

With square roots, first find the domain (the expression under the root must be non-negative), and only square both sides when both are known to be non-negative, by rule 4. This usually means splitting into cases.

blocks.title: Absolute values
blocks.solution:
(a) An absolute value is never negative, so a solution needs $x + 1 \ge 0$, and then the inequality says $-(x + 1) \le 2x - 3 \le x + 1$. The left part gives $3x \ge 2$, so $x \ge \frac23$; the right part gives $x \le 4$. Both force $x + 1 > 0$ automatically. Solution: $\left[\frac23, 4\right]$. Check at the ends: at $x = \frac23$ both sides equal $\frac53$; at $x = 4$ both equal 5.

(b) The expressions inside change sign at $x = 1$ and $x = -2$.

- If $x < -2$: the sum is $(1 - x) + (-x - 2) = -2x - 1 < 5$, so $x > -3$. This gives $(-3, -2)$.
- If $-2 \le x \le 1$: the sum is $(1 - x) + (x + 2) = 3 < 5$, always true. This gives $[-2, 1]$.
- If $x > 1$: the sum is $2x + 1 < 5$, so $x < 2$. This gives $(1, 2)$.

Together: $(-3, 2)$. Geometrically, $|x - 1| + |x + 2|$ is the total distance from $x$ to the points $1$ and $-2$. It equals 3 anywhere between them and grows by 2 for each unit you move outside, reaching 5 at $x = 2$ and $x = -3$.

blocks.title: A square root
blocks.body: Solve $\sqrt{x + 3} > x + 1$.
blocks.solution:
Domain: $x \ge -3$.

Case $x + 1 < 0$, that is $-3 \le x < -1$: the left side is at least 0 and the right side is negative, so the inequality holds. All of $[-3, -1)$ works.

Case $x + 1 \ge 0$, that is $x \ge -1$: both sides are non-negative, so squaring is allowed and gives an equivalent inequality: $x + 3 > x^2 + 2x + 1$, so $x^2 + x - 2 < 0$, so $(x + 2)(x - 1) < 0$, so $-2 < x < 1$. Combined with $x \ge -1$: $[-1, 1)$.

Solution: $[-3, 1)$. Check: at $x = 0$, $\sqrt3 > 1$; at $x = 1$, $2 > 2$ is false; at $x = 2$, $\sqrt5 > 3$ is false. Squaring without the case split would have produced $(-2, 1)$ and missed $[-3, -2]$.

blocks.title: Positive for every x
blocks.body: For which real $m$ is $x^2 - mx + m + 3 > 0$ for all real $x$?
blocks.solution:
The leading coefficient is $1 > 0$, so by the sign theorem the quadratic is positive for every $x$ exactly when it has no real root, that is when $\Delta < 0$. (If $\Delta = 0$ it equals 0 at the repeated root, and if $\Delta > 0$ it is negative between the roots.)

$$\Delta = m^2 - 4(m + 3) = m^2 - 4m - 12 = (m - 6)(m + 2) < 0 \iff -2 < m < 6.$$

Check the boundary $m = 6$: the quadratic is $x^2 - 6x + 9 = (x - 3)^2$, which is 0 at $x = 3$, so $m = 6$ is correctly excluded. An inequality about $x$ for all $x$ became an inequality about the parameter $m$.

blocks.title: Further: inequalities in two variables
blocks.body:
In the plane, a linear inequality $ax + by \le c$ (with $a, b$ not both 0) describes a half-plane: the line $ax + by = c$ and everything on one side of it. Test a point not on the line, such as the origin, to see which side. A system of several linear inequalities describes the intersection of half-planes, a convex polygonal region (possibly empty or unbounded).

For example $x \ge 0$, $y \ge 0$, $x + y \le 4$, $x + 2y \le 6$ is the quadrilateral with corners $(0, 0)$, $(4, 0)$, $(2, 2)$ and $(0, 3)$; the corner $(2, 2)$ is where the two slanted lines cross. To maximise $3x + 4y$ over this region, notice that the lines $3x + 4y = k$ are parallel, and the largest $k$ whose line still meets the region touches it at a corner. Evaluating at the corners gives $0, 12, 14, 12$, so the maximum is 14 at $(2, 2)$. This "check the corners" principle is the start of [[linear-programming]].

For a university reader: the rules at the top of the page follow from the axioms of an ordered field (see [[real-numbers]]), so they hold in $\mathbb{Q}$ as well as $\mathbb{R}$; the sign-chart method additionally uses that a polynomial can only change sign at a root, which over $\mathbb{R}$ is a consequence of factorisation or of the intermediate value theorem (see [[continuity]]).

- Multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the inequality; multiplying by an expression of unknown sign is not allowed without splitting into cases.
- Do not "cancel" a common factor: $x^2 > x$ does not mean $x > 1$; it means $x(x - 1) > 0$, so $x < 0$ or $x > 1$.
- Squaring both sides is safe only when both sides are non-negative.
- The solution of $x^2 < 9$ is $-3 < x < 3$, not $x < \pm 3$.
- Zeros of a denominator are never part of the solution, even for $\le$ or $\ge$.
- Taking reciprocals reverses an inequality only when both sides have the same sign: $-1 < 2$ but $-1 < \frac12$.

Systems of linear inequalities lead to [[linear-programming]] and, more generally, [[convex-optimisation]]. Proving that an inequality holds for all values, rather than solving it, is the subject of [[amgm]] and [[cauchy-schwarz]]. Absolute-value inequalities are the language of limits: the definition of a limit on [[limits]] asks you to solve $|x - a| < \delta$ so that $|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon$. Rational expressions and their sign charts reappear on [[rational-functions]].

1. Solve $3 - 2x \ge 5x - 11$ and $-1 \le \frac{3 - x}{2} < 4$.
2. Solve $x^3 - 4x^2 - 5x \le 0$ and $\dfrac{x^2 - 1}{x + 3} > 0$.
3. Solve $|x + 2| \ge 2x - 1$.
4. Find all $k$ for which $kx^2 + 4x + k > 0$ for every real $x$ (do not forget $k = 0$).

entry.sum: A rational function is a quotient $f(x) = p(x)/q(x)$ of polynomials, defined wherever $q(x) \ne 0$. After cancelling common factors, the zeros of the denominator give vertical asymptotes, cancelled factors leave holes, and the degrees of $p$ and $q$ decide the end behaviour. Every proper rational function splits uniquely into partial fractions, simple pieces with one linear or irreducible quadratic factor (or a power of one) in each denominator.
key: \frac{p(x)}{(x - a_1)\cdots(x - a_n)} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{A_i}{x - a_i}, \quad A_i = \frac{p(a_i)}{\prod_{j \ne i}(a_i - a_j)} \quad (\deg p < n,\ a_i \text{ distinct})
\deg p < \deg q \implies \lim_{x \to \pm\infty} \frac{p(x)}{q(x)} = 0
\frac{1}{k(k+1)} = \frac1k - \frac{1}{k+1}
entry.why: Rational functions are the simplest functions with asymptotes, and they model quantities like average cost or the strength of a lens. Partial fractions turn them into pieces that are easy to integrate, sum telescopically, or expand as power series, which is how one solves linear recurrences and inverts Laplace transforms.

links.note: Over the complex numbers a rational function is meromorphic, and the coefficients of the terms $A/(z - a)$ in its partial fraction expansion are its residues at the poles $a$.

A sequence satisfying a linear recurrence with constant coefficients has a rational generating function, and partial fractions turn it into an explicit formula such as Binet's formula for Fibonacci numbers.
Solving linear ODEs by the Laplace transform ends with a rational function of $s$, which partial fractions break into terms whose inverse transforms are known exponentials and sinusoids.
